title: Like as the waves ... (Ovid, Met. 15)
short: The opening quatrain adapts Pythagoras' speech in Ovid's Metamorphoses 15, where time flows like waves, each pushed on by the next.
body: In Metamorphoses 15.179-85 Ovid's Pythagoras says that time moves like a river: as wave is driven by wave, pressed by the one behind and pressing the one ahead, so the moments fly and follow at once and are always new. Golding's 1567 translation renders the passage in fourteeners Shakespeare knew. Bate argues the whole sonnet draws on Book 15, the three quatrains corresponding roughly to Ovid's passages on flux, the ages of man, and devouring time. 'Like as' is an old form of 'just as'. 'Make towards' means move towards. 'Pebbled' shore adds the sound of waves on shingle.

anchor: our minutes hasten to their end
title: our minutes ... sonnet number 60
short: Minutes hurry to their end; critics have noticed that 'minutes' appear in the sixtieth sonnet, as there are sixty minutes in an hour.
body: The surface sense is simple: the small units of our lives rush to their close, like waves to the shore. Critics have noted that this is Sonnet 60 and that it speaks of 'minutes', just as Sonnet 12 counts the clock's hours; Kerrigan makes the point in his Penguin introduction. Whether the 1609 ordering is numerically designed is debated, and the pairing may be coincidence. Dympna Callaghan links Sonnets 12 and 60 to the new mechanical clock-time, in her essay 'Confounded by Winter: Speeding Time in Shakespeare's Sonnets'.

title: sequent toil ... contend
short: Each wave or minute takes the place of the one before, labouring one after another, all struggling to press forward.
body: 'Sequent' means following in order, in succession (Latin sequi, to follow). 'Toil' and 'contend' make the movement effortful and combative, as if each moment strained against the others. Booth notes that words of struggle (toil, contend, fight, transfix, scythe) run through the poem and dramatize the war with Time. The line closely renders Ovid's image of each wave pressing and being pressed.

title: Nativity, once in the main of light
short: The newborn child, once it is out in the broad expanse of light (the world); 'main' also keeps the sea image of the first quatrain.
body: 'Nativity' (birth) stands for the newborn person. 'The main of light' is hard: 'main' means a broad expanse, especially the open sea (OED), so the phrase carries the waves of quatrain 1 into a 'sea of light', the world into which the baby is born. Tyler (1890) glosses it as the world imagined as a wide ocean lit by the sun. Editors also connect Ovid's 'editus in lucem' (born into the light, Met. 15.221), where the newborn lies helpless. Some hear a hint of the sun's course as well, preparing for 'eclipses'.

title: Crawls to maturity
short: The infant creeps slowly, like a crawling baby, toward adulthood.
body: The literal crawling of the infant becomes the slow, laborious ascent of a life. Tyler notes a sense of human abjection too, comparing Hamlet's 'crawling between earth and heaven'. The movement also suggests the sun climbing to its height at noon, in keeping with 'crown'd' and 'glory'. Ovid's account of the ages of man (Met. 15.221 ff.) moves similarly from helpless infancy through creeping childhood to strength and decline.

title: wherewith being crown'd
short: As soon as it reaches maturity, as though crowned at its peak, the life begins to be attacked.
body: 'Wherewith' means 'with which (maturity)'. Maturity is a crown, the height of life, like the sun at noon or a king at his coronation. The image of royal glory makes the next line's 'eclipses' and 'fight' read as a usurpation. Booth notes the merging of solar, regal and military images here. The grammar also allows a reading in which the crown is the very moment that triggers decline.

title: Crooked eclipses
short: Malignant eclipses (ill-omened in astrology) fight against the life's glory, as eclipses darken the sun.
body: In Elizabethan astrology eclipses were malign portents, bringing misfortune to rulers. 'Crooked' means perverse, malignant, twisted (OED), and may also hint at the bent shape of old age. Tyler glosses the phrase as adverse circumstances that turn a life from its course. 'His glory' refers to Nativity, i.e. the person at the height of life, now pictured as a sun or king obscured. Compare Sonnet 35 ('Clouds and eclipses stain both moon and sun').

title: confound
short: Time, who gave the gift of life and beauty, now destroys it.
body: 'Confound' in Shakespeare often means destroy, ruin, bring to nothing (OED), stronger than the modern 'confuse'. Time is both giver and destroyer, a classical paradox Ovid states in the same book (15.234: 'tempus edax rerum', time the devourer of things). The line ends the second quatrain's arc from birth to ruin. Tyler glosses it as 'spoil and render worthless his gift'.

anchor: transfix the flourish set on youth
title: transfix the flourish
short: Time pierces through (or removes) the bloom and ornament set upon youth.
body: 'Flourish' means a blossoming, bloom, and also a decorative ornament or embellishment (OED), so youth's beauty is both flower and added decoration. 'Transfix' usually means pierce through, as with a spear; editors debate whether Shakespeare also intends the Latin sense 'fix across', or a sense close to 'remove' or 'destroy'. Booth sets out the ambiguity and counts 'transfix' among the poem's violent words. Tyler glosses the line as 'doth kill and destroy youthful beauty'.

anchor: delves the parallels in beauty's brow
title: delves the parallels
short: Time digs parallel furrows, wrinkles, in the forehead of beauty.
body: 'Delves' means digs. The 'parallels' are the lines of wrinkles across the brow, imagined as trenches dug in a field or in siegeworks (in military usage 'parallels' were later the trenches dug in front of a besieged town). The image recalls Sonnet 2, 'And dig deep trenches in thy beauty's field'. Duncan-Jones and Burrow note the agricultural and military senses together. The action prepares for the scythe of l. 12.

title: Feeds on the rarities
short: Time devours the rarest and most perfect creations of nature, echoing Ovid's 'tempus edax rerum', time the eater of things.
body: Ovid's Pythagoras calls time 'edax rerum', devourer of things (Met. 15.234), the source of Shakespeare's 'devouring Time' in Sonnet 19. 'Rarities of nature's truth' are the rare, true perfections of nature, genuine beauty as opposed to cosmetic art, as Tyler explains. 'Truth' may also mean the fixed pattern or faithfulness of nature. Bate sets this line within the third Ovidian movement of the sonnet.

title: his scythe to mow
short: Nothing exists except to be cut down by Time's scythe, the attribute of Time as reaper.
body: Renaissance iconography gave Father Time a scythe, an attribute merged from the Greek Kronos (Saturn's sickle) and the harvest reaper; the figure is common in emblem books. 'Nothing stands but for' means nothing stands up except in order to be mown down. The image completes the farming sequence (delves, feeds, mow) of quatrain 3. Compare Sonnet 12 ('nothing 'gainst Time's scythe can make defence') and Sonnet 100, where the same instrument appears.

title: to times in hope ... my verse shall stand
short: Yet my verse will survive into future times (times hoped-for, still to come), praising you in spite of Time.
body: 'Times in hope' means future times, times that exist only in hope or expectation. Some editors hear 'in hope' as attaching to the verse too: the poet only hopes his verse will stand. 'Stand' answers 'nothing stands' in l. 12 directly. Vendler calls the couplet a reversing couplet that pushes back against the whole body of the poem; others read it as weaker than the twelve lines of destruction.
